title: Knowledge was worship
hookLine: scholars studied the stars and the body for the sake of Allah

cards: Standing. Sitting. Lying on your side.
The Qur'an describes people who remember God in all three positions, and then adds one more thing they do: they consider the creation of the heavens and the earth.

Remembering, then looking hard at the world, side by side in one verse. Through this year's history we've met astronomers, physicians, mapmakers, people who measured the sky and opened books on the eye.
It's easy to file them under science, a different drawer from prayer. The verse doesn't seem to keep two drawers. Today: knowledge was worship.

teach.b: Start with the verse, near the close of the third surah. The people of understanding remember Allah standing, sitting and reclining, they consider the heavens and the earth, and what comes out of their mouths is praise.
In Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain." The study ends in worship. Second, the body.

teach.h: EVERY DISEASE HAS A CURE: GO FIND IT.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet, peace be upon him, saying that God has not sent down a disease without sending down its cure.

Some readers heard that as a promise and an assignment at once: the cure exists, so go and find it. Physicians in Muslim lands wrote on the eye, on fevers, on the heart, and some saw the search as service.
Third, the same person. History keeps handing us people who don't fit one label.

teach.h: A JUDGE WHO WAS ALSO A PHYSICIAN.
teach.b: Ibn Rushd of Cordoba was a judge of Islamic law and a physician. Ibn Sina wrote a canon of medicine and also commentaries on chapters of the Qur'an.
For them the line between a religious subject and a worldly one wasn't drawn where a modern school timetable draws it.
Fourth, the intention. What turned study into worship wasn't the subject.

teach.h: THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.
teach.b: A scholar of grammar could study for fame; a pharmacist could study for God. The tradition kept asking what the work was for. That lesson reaches an ordinary desk too: a spreadsheet, a textbook, an engine manual.
Look hard enough, for the right reason, and the verse's last line is waiting at the end.

how: Muslims often begin study with the name of God and a renewed intention, and the Qur'an's plea for more knowledge (20:114) is one some students say before a lesson.

o: a judge of Islamic law in Cordoba
knowledge, which can be a form of worship
the canon of medicine Ibn Sina wrote

games.q: knowledge was worship — tap the pairs.

s: the verse about the heavens and the earth ends in praise
"Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain."
in the history, scholars of religion never studied medicine or the stars
Ibn Rushd was a judge of Islamic law and a physician; Ibn Sina wrote on medicine and on surahs of the Qur'an.
the subject decides whether study is worship
the tradition kept asking what the work was for: the intention.

games.q: you're a young physician who has just heard the hadith that God sent no disease without its cure. a fever is killing people in your town and nobody knows a remedy. what does the hadith suggest?
o: accept it; if a cure existed, someone would know it.
the cure exists; search for it.
games.why: some readers heard the hadith as both a promise and an assignment: the cure is there to be found.

practice: Look closely at your own hand the way an astronomer looks at a star: the lines across the palm, the joints, the pulse at the wrist under two fingers. Count nothing; just notice how much is there that you didn't make.
If you pray, end with the verse's own words, our Lord, You did not create this in vain; if not, simply study it for its own sake.

wordCard.voice: Ilm, the Arabic word for knowledge, studied by people like Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd as a form of worship when the intention is right. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: study as prayer. The intention, not the subject, makes it worship. Back tomorrow, same hill.
